HYPOTHESIS (data-grounded, answering "what kind of demographic disparities exist in median wealth in 1985 among individuals who were ever incarcerated"):

Among the 289 respondents ever incarcerated (jailed 1985–1994), 1985 median composite wealth is strongly stratified by race and sex. Within the incarcerated group, White men (n=57) hold the highest median wealth (≈$2,000), followed by Black men (n=143 — the largest incarcerated cell — ≈$800) and Hispanic men (n=52, ≈$700); the smaller female cells are low-reliability but point to the bottom of the distribution, with Black women (n=16) and Hispanic women (n=9) both at a median of ≈$0 (81% and 89% of those cells at zero or negative wealth) and White women (n=12) at ≈$4,100. This within-group gradient is compounded by who is disproportionately incarcerated: Black men are both the most heavily jailed (9.8% vs 1.6% for White men) and, before incarceration, already had lower 1985 median wealth (≈$1,500 vs ≈$5,500 for White men; Hispanic men ≈$5,000). Contextualized against the non-incarcerated, the incarcerated group's median 1985 wealth (≈$720) is only about one-fifth of the non-incarcerated median (≈$3,600), and the jailed-vs-not gap is largest for Hispanic men (≈$700 vs ≈$5,000). In short, the demographic disparity in 1985 median wealth among the ever-incarcerated is a race-and-sex gradient in which Black and Hispanic men — and, in smaller, less reliable cells, Black and Hispanic women — begin with the lowest median wealth, with Black men the most heavily incarcerated and among the poorest of the incarcerated men.

payload.workflow: Loaded data/nls_incarceration_processed.csv (12,013 rows × 6 columns; 0 missing in all columns). Treated the file's 'hipanic' as the single 'Hispanic' race category. Compared median composite_wealth_1985 for ever_jailed==1 (n=289, 2.41%) vs ever_jailed==0 (n=11,724). Computed 1985 median wealth within the incarcerated group by race, by sex, and by the race×sex interaction; computed the same interaction across both incarceration groups; and computed incarceration incidence (ever_jailed rate) by race×sex. Nonpositive wealth (32% of the sample ≤0; 27% exactly 0) was KEPT as-is in the primary median because net debt/zero are real states and the median is robust to the heavy right skew; a positive-wealth-only median was reported only as a sensitivity footnote (it narrows but does not erase the gap: ≈$5,600 jailed vs ≈$9,800 not-jailed). Headline uses the all-values median. Limitations/construct caveats: (a) ever_jailed is defined as 'jailed between 1985–1994' — a short-term jail indicator — and is used here as the only available proxy for 'ever incarcerated'; it is not a broader ever-incarcerated (incl. prison) measure and may under-count. (b) Temporal overlap: incarceration spans 1985–1994 but wealth is a 1985 snapshot, so 1985 wealth is pre-/concurrent wealth and a cross-sectional median comparison cannot establish causal direction (incarceration→wealth vs wealth→incarceration). (c) A residence-based incarceration proxy (e.g., 'in prison/jail at survey') cannot be constructed from the staged columns (no residence/location variable is present), so it was not approximated. (d) Incarcerated-female cells are small (n=9–16); their medians (several exactly 0) are low-reliability. (e) composite_wealth_1985 is an unnormalized sum of five wealth components that can be negative; it is suitable for median comparisons (robust) but is an overall-wealth index, not a market-value measure. Supporting code: analysis.py; full output: analysis_output.txt.
